title: Iron Age coins point to a female ruler behind Rome's invasion
dek: New research from Bournemouth University argues that Verica, the exiled ruler whose appeal to Claudius preceded the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43, was a woman. Coins bearing the title rex and a feminine image are central to the claim.
body: Verica ruled the Atrebates, a powerful tribe whose lands stretched across what is now Hampshire and West Sussex. Around AD 40 this ruler was forced from power and escaped to Rome to seek help from Emperor Claudius. The Roman historian Cassius Dio claimed that Verica's appeal was the reason Claudius decided to invade Britain. If accurate, that appeal helped set in motion one of the most consequential events in British history.

Dr. Miles Russell of Bournemouth University led the research and argues that earlier historians incorrectly identified Verica as male. He says the assumption came from the patriarchal mindset of nineteenth-century classical historians. Russell is Director of Archaeological Fieldwork at Bournemouth University and presents the findings in a new book published by Bloomsbury.

Russell points to the name Verica itself, which ends in the letter a, a feature common among female names of the time. He compares it with Cartimandua, who ruled the Brigantes in Yorkshire, and Boudica, leader of the Iceni in Norfolk. All three rulers lived during roughly the same period, though Boudica is better known because of her rebellion against Roman rule in AD 60.

Coins issued under Verica's rule bear the Latin title rex, traditionally translated as king. Russell explains that rex was not necessarily restricted to men and notes that both male and female rulers were recognized by Rome, with Cleopatra of Egypt as the most famous example. He adds that the title shows Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor.

The artwork on the coins provides another clue. Rather than depicting the masculine warriors found on coins from other British Iron Age leaders, Verica's coins show a slender, feminine, bare-breasted figure riding on horseback. Russell argues this visual evidence should be taken at face value.

Russell believes Verica may have been a valuable political and military ally who supplied the Romans with intelligence and practical assistance. He suggests Cassius Dio's account reinforced a negative portrayal of Claudius as easily influenced by women. In this reading, Verica provided the excuse for regime change, and the emperor seized it to supports himself as a military leader.

The research builds on earlier Bournemouth University work exploring the position of women in ancient British society, including a study indicating that husbands moved into their wives' communities after marriage. Together these findings prompt researchers to reconsider the influence women may have exercised in Iron Age Britain.
doesnt_show: The article does not show when the coins were excavated, where they were found, or how they were dated. It does not present independent scientific tests or peer-reviewed publication of the coin evidence.
settle: Independent archaeological dating and metallurgical analysis of the coins, published in a peer-reviewed journal, would settle whether they support the identification of Verica as female.
